description: No existe un camino único hacia la verdad. La ciencia nos da el poder de explorar cada posibilidad, cuestionar lo establecido y seguir avanzando hasta encontrar la respuesta. Porque descubrir no es seguir un camino, es atreverse a crear uno.
summary: The Last Hope is a prototype health and wellbeing companion for astronauts, designed to run on the laptops crews already use on the ISS and, later, on missions to the Moon and Mars. It shows each crew member’s health on an interactive 3D body. Astronauts can tap any zone to see the organs and 32 indicators, compare their data with their own pre-flight history and with past missions using published NASA research, and follow daily care routines adapted to the mission. At its core is ALVA, an onboard companion astronauts can talk to by voice or text. It offers emotional support, uses health data only with the astronaut’s permission, never diagnoses, and redirects anyone in distress to the flight surgeon. This matters because on long missions, communication delays and isolation mean crews can’t rely on real-time help from Earth. The Last Hope works offline, helps detect health changes early and supports mental health, giving every crew a way to look after body and mind far from home.
details: The Last Hope is a prototype health and wellbeing companion designed to run on the laptops astronauts already use on the ISS, and later on missions to the Moon and Mars. It shows each crew member’s health on an interactive 3D body: tap any zone and the skin opens to reveal the organs, with 32 indicators explaining what each value means, where it comes from, and what it cannot conclude. It also offers daily challenges and care routines adapted to the mission, and compares each astronaut with their own pre-flight history and with reference values from past missions based on published NASA research. Its heart is ALVA, a voice-and-text companion that talks like a person, uses health data only when relevant and only with the astronaut’s permission, remembers only what it’s asked to, never diagnoses, and redirects anyone in distress to the flight surgeon. Because a Mars crew can face delays of up to about 20 minutes each way to Earth, our goal is to give every crew an offline tool that watches over both physical and mental health, with clear benefits for early detection, privacy and psychological support, and possible uses in remote places on Earth. We built it with JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Python and Three.js with custom GLSL shaders. AI conversation runs through OpenRouter, and ElevenLabs provides ALVA’s AI-generated voice and speech recognition. It runs as a no-install desktop app, a website or a standalone HTML file, using simulated wearable data modeled on biometric shirts like the Astroskin, and is tested with 14 automated tests. Along the way we weighed safety, consent, honesty about data quality, crew time, accessibility, and a realistic path to flight certification, which we estimate at roughly US$0.9–2.2 million.
